newsitem.title: USA: Washington yawns after EU statement on Boeing.
newsitem.headline: Washington yawns after EU statement on Boeing.

text.p: Official Washington reacted with a yawn on Thursday to the European Union's announcement of formal objections to the proposed $14 billion merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp.

"This was not a surprise to anyone, given the public statements that have been made," one White House official said. "We're going to let the Federal Trade Commission act. Their decision is expected in early July."

The FTC will decide whether the merger is permissible under U.S. antitrust laws. The FTC had no reaction to Wednesday's announcement by European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert objecting to the merger.
Van Miert cited recent exclusive sales deals negotiated by Boeing that have shut out Europe's Airbus Industrie consortium, among other concerns.

The U.S. Trade Representative's office had nothing new to say either. The office, which negotiates trade policy, has said it would watch the European Union's actions in the case very closely to gauge whether they were fair and impartial.
The EU statement sets the stage for hearings in Europe with Boeing next month. A final decision is expected by August.
One veteran airline analyst discounted the strident tone in both the European and U.S. comments on the case.

"I don't think anybody wants a trade war but everybody is posturing right now to try to get as good a deal as they can," said Darryl Jenkins, a professor at George Washington University who runs the Consultancy Aviation Foundation in Falls Church, Va.

Noting that Boeing is the biggest U.S. exporter and that Airbus includes companies from four European countries, Jenkins said the concerns on both sides are "not positioning for a trade war. It's taking care of your constituent interests."
He said the EU "just wants to make sure Airbus can compete in a global market. And that's what it should be."

No one mentioned concerns, expressed by some outside the government, that the European Union would have the power to impose a fine equal to 10 percent of the revenue of Boeing and McDonnell Douglas. Such a fine could be imposed only if the two companies merged in defiance of the EU.
Officials on both sides of the Atlantic have said that was unlikely.
Boeing said on Wednesday after receiving the EU statement that it fully expected an agreement could be worked out.
Separately, a spokeswoman for Airbus in the United States said the company would "seriously consider" exclusive purchase agreements that Van Miert objected to in the EU statement.

"Airbus will always try to fill market demand," the spokeswoman said. "We would consider (exclusive agreements) seriously. We do obviously object to the exclusive deals -- we think they're anticompetitive -- but so far they're not against the law.

Van Miert has said the EU cannot permit the Boeing-McDonnell merger as long as Boeing has exclusive 20-year provider agreements with American Airlines and Delta Air Lines Inc. Boeing reportedly is negotiating another, similar deal with Continental.
Critics have argued that Airbus has its own exclusive deal with US Airways but the airline said recently Boeing was a potential supplier.
